commitResults.messageBody: Include the project-local present-changes-visually skill and its standard-library HTML diff generator so future reviews can compare Git revisions without modifying source files.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add text-UI testing skill and require it after code changes
commitResults.messageBody:
Kenbot is a console program, so the cheapest meaningful regression check is
to type commands into it and compare what it prints. Until now there was no
such check, and no rule saying when to run one.

Add the project-local test-ui skill, which compiles the sources into a
temporary folder and runs each test case as a fresh program run, feeding it
the case's input lines and comparing the whole console output. The session
stops at the first failure and reports the expected output, the actual
output, and the difference between them, because later results cannot be
trusted once the program is misbehaving.

Record the test cases in test/ui-test-plan.md rather than inside the runner,
so they stay readable and reviewable. Each case states its aim, its input
lines, and its expected output; the shared greeting banner is recorded once
and prepended automatically. The plan also lists the behaviours that are
deliberately untested because the program currently crashes rather than
printing anything expectable.

Add a "Testing workflow after code changes" section to AGENTS.md so both
Codex and Claude update the plan and run the tests after every change to
src/main/java, without being asked. CLAUDE.md already imports AGENTS.md, so
one section covers both agents.

Re-include .claude/skills/ in .gitignore, since a global gitignore excludes
.claude/ and would otherwise keep the skill out of the repository.

commitResults.messageTitle: Share skills between Claude Code and Codex via symlinks
commitResults.messageBody:
This project is worked on with Claude Code today but may be worked on with
Codex later, so the two must have identical functionality. That was not the
case: present-changes-visually existed only under .codex/skills/, and the
new test-ui skill existed only under .claude/skills/, so each agent could
run one of the two.

Make .codex/skills/ the single home for every skill and symlink each one
into .claude/skills/. A symlink rather than a second copy, so the two can
never drift: there is one set of files, one place to edit, and one thing to
review. Git records these as symlinks, so a fresh clone gets both agents'
views without any extra setup.

Move test-ui to .codex/skills/test-ui/ and symlink both skills into
.claude/skills/. Rewrite the documented runner command to use the .codex/
path, which resolves under either agent, and note the shared layout in the
skill itself.

Add a "Skills must work in both Claude Code and Codex" section to AGENTS.md
recording the rule, the symlink command, and the requirement to check that a
new skill runs from both paths before calling it done.

Verified: the full text-UI plan passes when run through either path.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a delete command for removing tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
Level 6 asks for tasks to be removable, and the A-Collections extension
asks for a Java collection rather than a plain array. TaskList already
holds an ArrayList, so only the command itself was missing.

Add TaskList.delete, which reuses the same validation as mark and unmark,
so a missing, non-numeric, out-of-range or zero task number is reported in
wording consistent with those commands, and deleting from an empty list
says so rather than quoting a range. Because the check is shared, the
delete command needed no error handling of its own.

Change the private helper from returning the task to returning its
position, and rename it from get to indexOf to match. Delete then removes
by position instead of by object, so it does not depend on how tasks
compare to each other. That matters if Task is ever given an equals
method, since removing by object would then be free to remove a different
task with the same contents.

Report the removal through printBlock like every other message, so the
separator lines and the indent in front of the task match the rest of the
program.

Expand the text-UI test plan from 19 cases to 26. The added cases cover
deleting from the middle and from the start to check that the remaining
tasks are renumbered, emptying the list, each way a delete number can be
rejected, and a run that interleaves adds, deletes and marks to confirm
the count follows the list rather than the number of tasks ever created.

Verified: all 26 cases pass. An off-by-one deliberately introduced into
delete was caught by TC20, which reported that the event was removed
instead of the deadline.

commitResults.messageTitle: Handle erroneous inputs and bug fixes

commitResults.messageBody:
# Conflicts:
#	src/main/java/kenbot/CommandType.java
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Several assumptions in the code are relied on but written down nowhere.
The index returned by TaskList#indexOf goes straight to ArrayList#get
without a second check, the message built by Kenbot#respondTo is shown
by both front ends without a null check, and TaskDate stores an absent
time as an empty string rather than null. Break any of these and the
failure appears far from its cause, as an out-of-bounds error or an
empty dialog box with nothing to explain it.

Record each assumption as an assertion, so a violation names the broken
expectation where it breaks:

* TaskList#indexOf: the index returned is within the list
* TaskList(List): Storage supplies a list, never null
* Kenbot#respondTo: every command produces something to show the user
* TaskDate: an absent time is empty, never null

These describe internal state only. Anything the user can cause is
still refused with a KenbotException, because the JVM ignores
assertions unless -ea is given and a check that can vanish is no
defence.

For the same reason, enable assertions for the run task and for the
text-UI test runner, both of which ran without them. The test task
already had them on, so the JUnit suite was the only place they were
live.
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

describe() and find() each built a numbered list of tasks with their
own StringBuilder and their own loop. The two produced the same
layout, so any change to how a task line is numbered or separated had
to be made correctly in both places, and nothing forced them to stay
in step.

Both now call one private formatNumbered helper, which is the single
place that decides that layout. find() also gains a plain list of
matches, which removes the found counter that was serving as both the
running number and the "nothing matched" flag.

Output is unchanged: all 47 JUnit tests and all 31 text-UI cases pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

The switch in respondTo named a step for seven of its nine commands
but assembled the reply text itself for mark and unmark, mixing two
levels of abstraction in one fragment. A reader following the switch
had to drop into wording details for those two arms and back out
again for the rest.

Both now call a helper, matching addTask and deleteTask, which were
already doing exactly this for the other commands. That also closes a
naming gap: mark and unmark were the only two operations without a
corresponding ...Task method, and the helpers are declared in the
order the switch uses them.

No behaviour change: all 47 JUnit tests and all 31 text-UI cases pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Event.of decided all three of its failure cases in one five-clause
condition, and needed a ternary producing an empty array purely so
that condition could index into the second split without crashing
when the first one had already failed.

It now checks one thing at a time and throws as soon as something is
wrong, which removes the dummy array and lets each split be read
against the guard that protects it. The three parts are named before
use, so the final line says TaskDate.of(start) rather than
TaskDate.of(toParts[0]) -- an index named after /to that in fact held
the /from value.

The message is now a constant because three guards report it. Old and
new were compiled side by side and produced identical output for ten
event inputs, including reversed and blank parts; all 47 JUnit tests
and all 31 text-UI cases pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Both FXML loads caught IOException, printed the stack trace and
carried on. In DialogBox that left dialog and displayPicture null, so
the next two lines failed with a NullPointerException mentioning
neither the file nor the original cause. In Main it was quieter
still: start() returned normally without ever reaching stage.show(),
leaving the toolkit running with no window and nothing on screen to
say why.

Both now wrap the cause in UncheckedIOException, the JDK class meant
for an IOException that cannot be declared. Neither site can recover:
the FXML is packaged inside the JAR, so a failure there is a broken
build, not something a user can act on.

The GUI was launched from the packaged JAR to check the window still
opens; all 47 JUnit tests and all 31 text-UI cases pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add tags to the task model
commitResults.messageBody:
A tag is a value class rather than a plain String so that a task can hold
its tags in a Set and ignore a repeat without checking for one itself, and
so that the rules about what a tag may contain live in one place. Storage
builds tags from the save file without going through Parser, so Tag.of
validates independently rather than relying on the command line having
been checked.

Tags have to print after a deadline's (by: ...), but each subclass wrapped
super.toString(), which left the parent no way to append anything after
the child's part. Task now owns the whole line and asks the subclass for
its middle through getTypeCode, getDisplayDetails and getStorableDetails.
That also removes the three-way repetition of the "[X]" + super pattern.

Only a run of # words at the end of an argument is tags, so "read #1 book"
keeps its #1. The rule lives in Tag.splitTrailingTags and is called by all
three of() methods before /by and /from are looked for, so the task types
cannot drift apart on it and never see a tag themselves.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Tags are written as one extra field at the end of a saved line, and only
when a task has any. A task without tags therefore produces exactly the
line it produced before tags existed, which is what lets an existing
data/Kenbot.txt be opened by this version with no migration step and no
tasks lost.

requireFieldCount demanded an exact count, so any new field would have
made every old line unreadable and silently skipped. It now accepts the
count for that task type or one more, the one more being the tag field.
Counts are 3 or 4 for a todo, 4 or 5 for a deadline, 5 or 6 for an event.

Names are stored without their #, since the field position already says
what they are, and separated by spaces, which is unambiguous because a
tag may not contain one.

A line ending in a bare separator is not an error: String.split drops a
trailing empty field, so it reads as an ordinary untagged task. Keeping
the task is better than discarding it over a stray separator, and there
is now a test recording that alongside one for a genuinely blank field.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Add tagging

The root AnchorPane carried maxHeight and maxWidth of -Infinity, which
in JavaFX means USE_PREF_SIZE. That capped the pane at 400x600 however
large the window grew, so maximising left the conversation in a narrow
column with empty space beside it.

Those two attributes are gone, and every child is now anchored instead
of being placed with layoutX/layoutY: the scroll pane fills all four
sides down to the input row, the text field stretches to the button,
and the button holds the bottom right corner. Measured at 400x600,
1200x800 and 1920x1080, each control tracks the window.

A dialog box no longer carries a fixed 400px width, so it spans
whatever the scroll pane gives it, and the message label is bound to
six tenths of that width so a long reply wraps rather than running the
full width of a large screen. The stage gains minimum bounds so it
cannot be dragged smaller than a usable size.

All 89 JUnit tests and all 40 text-UI cases pass; the packaged JAR was
launched to confirm the window still opens.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Make the window resize properly

The conversation is between a person and a program, not between two
people, so showing both sides in the same format implied a symmetry
that is not there. What the user typed is now a small tinted bubble on
the right with no picture at all, since the user knows who they are and
the space is better spent on the reply; Kenbot's side keeps the picture
and gets the wider bubble and the higher contrast.

The pictures are clipped to circles and cut from 99px to 40px. At the
old size two of them and their padding took more vertical room than the
message between them, which is the wrong way round for a window whose
whole job is showing text.

Styling moves out of the FXML into css/main.css and css/dialog-box.css,
so the shape of the window and the look of it can be changed
independently. A stylesheet that fails to resolve is silent in JavaFX,
so the applied colours were read back from a laid-out scene rather than
assumed: user #3478f6, reply white, both pictures clipped.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Every reply looked the same, so a refusal was indistinguishable from a
result until the user read it. Kenbot now records whether the last reply
reported a problem, and the window shows those in red with an outline.

The outline is not decoration: colour alone would leave anyone who
cannot easily separate red from grey with no signal at all, so the
border carries the same information a second time.

The flag is kept on Kenbot rather than returned beside the text, so the
console front end, which shows both kinds the same way, is not made to
handle a value it would ignore. Seven tests cover it, including that a
later good command clears it and a later bad one sets it again.

The user guide's claim that the window cannot be resized was also left
over from before the anchors were fixed, and is corrected here.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Kenbot had a personality in exactly two places, the greeting and the
farewell, and stock wording everywhere in between. Around thirty
messages now read in the same register: short, spoken, contractions,
no exclamation pile-ups and no phrasing a person would not use out
loud.

Error messages keep their format hints, since that is the useful part
of them. Only the framing changed: "Tell me which task to mark, like:
mark 2" became "Which task to mark? Like: mark 2".

The running total was also wrong. "Now you have 1 tasks in the list."
said "1 tasks" for a single task, and both adding and removing repeated
the sentence. It is now built in one place and pluralised, so it reads
"That makes 1 task." or "That makes 3 tasks."

Every expected output moved with the wording rather than being adjusted
to match whatever the program happened to print: 40 text-UI cases, the
JUnit assertions in four test classes, and the worked examples in the
user guide. All 96 JUnit tests and all 40 text-UI cases pass, and the
documented examples were re-run against the program to confirm the
guide still shows what actually appears.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
